questions.q: Where in the cell does glycolysis take place?
questions.exp: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not require oxygen, so it can run in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions.
optExp: The matrix hosts the TCA cycle and link reaction, not glycolysis.
ETC complexes sit here; glycolysis is cytosolic.
DNA replication/transcription happens here, not glycolysis.
The smooth ER handles lipid synthesis, not glucose breakdown.

questions.q: What is the NET ATP yield from glycolysis of one glucose molecule?
questions.exp: Glycolysis invests 2 ATP and generates 4 ATP, giving a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose.
optExp: 4 is the gross production, not the net yield.
8 ATP exceeds glycolytic output; this is closer to total NADH equivalents.
6 ATP would require including TCA-derived molecules.
38 ATP is the approximate yield from complete glucose oxidation, not glycolysis alone.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting step of glycolysis?
opts: Pyruvate kinase catalyses final pyruvate formation
Aldolase catalyses aldol cleavage of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
questions.exp: PFK-1 catalyses the irreversible conversion of F6P to F1,6BP and is allosterically regulated by ATP, AMP, citrate, and F2,6BP — making it the rate-limiting step.
optExp: Hexokinase is irreversible but not the rate-limiting committed step.
Pyruvate kinase is irreversible but not rate-limiting.
Aldolase catalyses a reversible cleavage and is not regulated.
Phosphoglyceromutase is a reversible enzyme and not the rate-limiting step.

questions.q: PFK-1 is allosterically INHIBITED by which of the following?
questions.exp: When ATP is abundant the cell does not need to make more, so high ATP allosterically inhibits PFK-1, slowing glycolysis.
optExp: AMP activates PFK-1, signalling low energy.
F2,6BP is the most potent activator of PFK-1.
Insulin upregulates glycolysis, not inhibits it.

questions.q: What are the NET products of glycolysis from one glucose molecule?
questions.exp: Per glucose: 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP (4 made − 2 invested), and 2 NADH are produced.
optExp: 4 ATP is gross output; 4 NADH overstates yield.
Acetyl-CoA is the product of the link reaction, not glycolysis.
FADH₂ is produced in the TCA cycle, not glycolysis.

questions.q: How many ATP are consumed in the investment phase of glycolysis?
questions.exp: Two ATP are invested: one by hexokinase (glucose → G6P) and one by PFK-1 (F6P → F1,6BP).
optExp: At least 1 ATP is needed for glucose phosphorylation.
Only one phosphorylation step would leave glucose unable to split.
4 ATP describes the gross gain, not investment.

questions.q: Which enzyme converts phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate in the final step of glycolysis?
questions.exp: Pyruvate kinase catalyses the irreversible transfer of phosphate from PEP to ADP, producing ATP and pyruvate.
optExp: Aldolase cleaves F1,6BP into two trioses.
Enolase converts 2-phosphoglycerate to PEP (the step before).
Hexokinase acts at the start, phosphorylating glucose.

questions.q: In anaerobic conditions, how is NAD⁺ regenerated so glycolysis can continue?
opts: Lactate dehydrogenase catalyses pyruvate to lactate conversion
questions.exp: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate, oxidising NADH back to NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep producing ATP.
optExp: The TCA cycle requires oxygen indirectly via NADH reoxidation.
The ETC requires O₂ as the terminal electron acceptor.
Beta-oxidation produces NADH, it does not regenerate NAD⁺.

questions.q: ATP hydrolysis (ATP → ADP + Pi) releases approximately how much free energy?
questions.exp: Hydrolysis of the terminal phosphoanhydride bond of ATP releases about −7.3 kcal/mol under standard conditions.
optExp: Too low — this is closer to weaker bond energies.
Roughly double; this is too high for a single phosphate hydrolysis.
Too low to drive most endergonic biological reactions.
Far too high; no single ATP bond releases this much.

questions.q: Which best describes an exergonic reaction?
questions.exp: Exergonic reactions are spontaneous, release free energy, and have a negative ΔG.
optExp: Contradictory: positive ΔG cannot release energy.
Contradictory: negative ΔG cannot require energy input.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes anabolism?
opts: Breaking down complex molecules into simpler units
Synthesizing complex molecules from simpler precursors
Converting glucose to pyruvate in glycolysis
Producing NADH in the tricarboxylic acid cycle
questions.exp: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller precursors and requires ATP input (endergonic).
optExp: Oxidative phosphorylation is catabolic energy production.

questions.q: Hexokinase differs from glucokinase in that hexokinase:
opts: Found mainly in hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells
Has high Km for glucose and lower substrate affinity
Has low Km and high affinity for glucose
Inducible by insulin in response to feeding
Not inhibited by its product glucose-6-phosphate
questions.exp: Hexokinase is present in most tissues with a low Km, ensuring efficient glucose uptake even at low blood glucose. Glucokinase (liver/β-cells) has a high Km and works after meals.
optExp: Hexokinase IS inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate (product inhibition).

questions.q: In red blood cells, why does glycolysis end with lactate production even when oxygen is available?
opts: Red blood cells lack mitochondria and cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation
Red blood cells lack glucose transporters on their membranes
Red blood cells have very high ATP demand relative to their size
Red blood cells cannot synthesize NADH from glycolysis
Red blood cells exclusively metabolize fatty acids for energy
questions.exp: Erythrocytes lack mitochondria, so they cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation and must regenerate NAD⁺ via lactate production.
optExp: RBC ATP demand is modest, but they still rely on glycolysis.
RBCs do make NADH in glycolysis.
RBCs rely on glucose, not fatty acids, for energy.

questions.q: The Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) of a reaction with ΔG < 0 is:
opts: Exergonic reaction, spontaneous under standard conditions
Endergonic reaction, non-spontaneous under standard conditions
Endergonic reaction, spontaneous under standard conditions
Exergonic reaction, non-spontaneous under standard conditions
questions.exp: Negative ΔG means the reaction is spontaneous and releases free energy.

questions.q: Which molecule is the most potent allosteric ACTIVATOR of PFK-1?
opts: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent allosteric activator
ATP is a potent allosteric inhibitor of PFK-1
Citrate is a potent allosteric inhibitor of PFK-1
NADH is a potent allosteric inhibitor of PFK-1
Acetyl-CoA is a potent allosteric inhibitor of PFK-1
questions.exp: F2,6BP, produced by PFK-2 in response to insulin, is the most potent activator of PFK-1 and stimulates glycolysis after meals.
optExp: NADH is not a PFK regulator.
Acetyl-CoA does not regulate PFK-1 directly.

questions.q: What is the immediate product of pyruvate kinase?
questions.exp: Pyruvate kinase transfers a phosphate from PEP to ADP, producing pyruvate and ATP.
optExp: Lactate is produced later by LDH if anaerobic.
Acetyl-CoA is from the link reaction.
PEP is the SUBSTRATE, not the product.
OAA is a TCA intermediate, not a glycolysis product.

questions.q: What is the role of NAD⁺ in glycolysis?
questions.exp: GAPDH oxidises glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, reducing NAD⁺ to NADH.
optExp: NAD⁺ is an electron carrier, not a phosphate donor.
Substrate-level phosphorylation involves PGK/PK, not NAD⁺.
NAD⁺ has no structural role with pyruvate.

questions.q: Catabolism is best described as:
questions.exp: Catabolism breaks larger molecules into smaller units, releasing energy in the form of ATP and reducing equivalents.
optExp: Phosphorylation can be either anabolic or catabolic.
This is one specific step in oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.q: Where does the TCA cycle take place?
questions.exp: Both the link reaction and the TCA cycle occur in the mitochondrial matrix.
optExp: ETC pumps protons here; TCA does not run here.
The ETC sits here, not TCA enzymes.
Only the outer membrane sits here; no TCA reactions.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the link reaction (pyruvate → acetyl-CoA)?
questions.exp: PDH oxidatively decarboxylates pyruvate, producing acetyl-CoA, CO₂, and NADH.
optExp: Pyruvate kinase acts in glycolysis, making pyruvate from PEP.
IDH is the TCA rate-limiting enzyme; comes later.
Citrate synthase joins acetyl-CoA to OAA inside the TCA.
α-KG dehydrogenase acts on α-KG within the TCA cycle.

questions.q: What are the products of the link reaction?
questions.exp: PDH converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing one CO₂ and producing one NADH per pyruvate.
optExp: FADH₂ is not produced by PDH.
No water is produced as a labelled product here.

questions.q: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of the TCA cycle?
questions.exp: Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyses the rate-limiting step. It is activated by ADP and inhibited by ATP/NADH.
optExp: Citrate synthase is regulated but not the rate-limiting step.
MDH catalyses the last step but is not rate-limiting.
Aconitase is a freely reversible isomerisation step.

questions.q: What are the products of ONE complete turn of the TCA cycle?
questions.exp: Per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP/ATP, 2 CO₂ — the '3211' rule.

questions.q: Isocitrate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by:
questions.exp: ADP signals low cellular energy and activates IDH, accelerating the TCA cycle.
optExp: Acetyl-CoA activates PDH but not IDH directly.
OAA is a substrate downstream, not an allosteric activator.

questions.q: Which enzyme joins oxaloacetate with acetyl-CoA at the start of the TCA cycle?
questions.exp: Citrate synthase condenses 4C OAA with 2C acetyl-CoA to form 6C citrate.
optExp: Isocitrate dehydrogenase acts later, on isocitrate.
Aconitase isomerises citrate to isocitrate — it does not form citrate.
Succinyl-CoA synthetase makes GTP further along.

questions.q: The Cori cycle transports which substrate from muscle to liver for re-conversion to glucose?
questions.exp: Lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in muscle is exported to the liver, where gluconeogenesis converts it back to glucose.
optExp: Fatty acids are not part of the Cori cycle.
Acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to glucose — it is irreversibly committed to the TCA cycle.
Alanine is the substrate of the glucose-alanine cycle, not the Cori cycle.
Glycerol enters gluconeogenesis but is not exported from muscle via the Cori cycle.

questions.q: Acetyl-CoA entering the TCA cycle can come from each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Lactate must first be converted back to pyruvate, then via PDH to acetyl-CoA — there is no direct lactate → acetyl-CoA step.
optExp: This is the standard PDH route.
Ketogenic amino acids (leucine, lysine) yield acetyl-CoA.
Ketone bodies can be reconverted to acetyl-CoA in extrahepatic tissues.

questions.q: How many CO₂ molecules are released per turn of the TCA cycle (excluding link reaction)?
questions.exp: Two CO₂ molecules are released per turn — by IDH (isocitrate → α-KG) and α-KG dehydrogenase (α-KG → succinyl-CoA).
optExp: 3 would include the link reaction's CO₂.
Excessive; only 2 decarboxylating steps in the cycle proper.
CO₂ IS released in the TCA cycle.

questions.q: Where is the electron transport chain located?
questions.exp: Complexes I-V of the ETC are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, allowing proton pumping into the intermembrane space.
optExp: The matrix hosts TCA enzymes, not the ETC.
Glycolysis is cytoplasmic; the ETC is not.
The outer membrane is permeable to ions and lacks ETC complexes.
DNA replication occurs here, not the ETC.

questions.q: What is the final electron acceptor of the ETC?
questions.exp: Oxygen accepts electrons at Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) and combines with H⁺ to form water.
optExp: NAD⁺ accepts electrons in the TCA cycle, not the end of ETC.
FAD acts at substrate level, not the end of ETC.
CO₂ is a waste product, not an electron acceptor.
Cytochrome c is an intermediate mobile carrier, not final.

questions.q: Which complex accepts electrons from NADH?
questions.exp: NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I) oxidises NADH and passes electrons to coenzyme Q while pumping 4 H⁺.
optExp: Complex II accepts electrons from FADH₂, not NADH.
Complex III receives from coenzyme Q.
Complex IV receives from cytochrome c.
Complex V is ATP synthase, not an electron transfer complex.

questions.q: Which mobile carrier transports electrons from Complex I/II to Complex III?
questions.exp: Coenzyme Q is a lipid-soluble quinone that shuttles electrons through the inner membrane to Complex III.
optExp: Cytochrome c transports between Complex III and IV.
NADH delivers electrons but is not mobile within the membrane.
FADH₂ is tethered to Complex II.
Iron-sulfur clusters are within complexes, not mobile.

questions.q: The mechanism by which proton flow through ATP synthase drives ATP production is called:
questions.exp: Chemiosmosis is the use of the proton gradient (proton-motive force) across the inner mitochondrial membrane to power ATP synthesis.
optExp: This describes direct phosphate transfer in glycolysis/TCA.
Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ but does not produce ATP from a gradient.

questions.q: Approximately how many ATP are produced from complete oxidation of one glucose molecule?
questions.exp: Complete oxidation yields ~30-38 ATP: 2 from glycolysis, 2 from TCA SLP, and the rest from oxidative phosphorylation.
optExp: 2 ATP is the glycolytic yield alone.

questions.q: Why do fats yield more energy per gram than carbohydrates?
opts: Fatty acids generate more NADH and FADH₂ per molecule
Lipids enter the TCA cycle directly
questions.exp: Fatty acids are highly reduced; beta-oxidation generates abundant NADH and FADH₂, producing ~9 kcal/g vs ~4 kcal/g for carbohydrates.
optExp: Lipids contain LESS oxygen than carbohydrates.
Fatty acids must be processed via beta-oxidation first.
Lipids still rely on oxidative phosphorylation.
Glycerol enters glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, not ATP directly.

questions.q: Cyanide inhibits oxidative phosphorylation by binding to:
questions.exp: Cyanide binds the Fe³⁺ in cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), preventing electron transfer to oxygen and stopping the ETC.
optExp: Malonate is a Complex II inhibitor.
Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase, not cyanide.

questions.q: Uncoupling agents (e.g. DNP, thermogenin in brown fat) cause:
opts: Loss of the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane
questions.exp: Uncouplers allow protons to leak back across the membrane without going through ATP synthase, dissipating the gradient as heat.
optExp: TCA may speed up to compensate.

questions.q: Brown adipose tissue generates heat via:
opts: UCP1 uncouples oxidative phosphorylation to dissipate energy as heat
Increased glycolysis in brown adipose tissue
questions.exp: Thermogenin (UCP1) allows protons to bypass ATP synthase, dissipating the gradient as heat — important in neonates.
optExp: Glycolysis is not a major heat source in BAT.
Beta-oxidation feeds fuel but doesn't itself uncouple.
Substrate cycles consume ATP but are not the main mechanism.
CYP450 is for drug metabolism, not thermogenesis.

questions.q: ATP synthase (Complex V) uses what to drive ATP synthesis?
opts: Proton gradient flowing down its electrochemical gradient
questions.exp: H⁺ flow from the intermembrane space back to the matrix through ATP synthase drives rotation and ATP synthesis.
optExp: Electron flow happens at I-IV, not V.
NADH oxidation is at Complex I.

questions.q: In oxidative phosphorylation, oxygen is reduced to:
questions.exp: At Complex IV, O₂ accepts four electrons and combines with 4 H⁺ to form 2 H₂O.
optExp: CO₂ is produced in TCA and link reaction, not the ETC.
H₂O₂ may form as a side product but is not the main product.
Superoxide can form as a leak but is detoxified.
Ozone is not a biological product.

questions.q: How do enzymes accelerate reactions?
opts: Lower the activation energy of the reaction
questions.exp: Enzymes lower the activation energy (Ea), allowing reactions to proceed faster without changing ΔG.
optExp: Enzymes do not shift equilibrium position.
They lower, not raise, energy barriers.

questions.q: An apoenzyme is:
opts: Inactive enzyme lacking a required cofactor or coenzyme
Active enzyme bound to its cofactor
questions.exp: Apoenzyme = protein-only, inactive. Apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme (active).
optExp: Denatured enzymes are permanently inactive; apoenzymes can be reactivated.
Number of active sites is unrelated.
Regulatory subunits are different structural elements.

questions.q: The induced fit model states that:
opts: The active site changes shape upon substrate binding
The active site is permanently rigid
Substrate molds to fit a rigid active site
Enzymes bind any substrate with equal affinity
The active site remains open and unchanging
questions.exp: In induced fit, the active site flexibly remodels around the substrate, optimising catalysis.
optExp: Rigid fit is the older 'lock and key' model.
The enzyme changes, not the substrate.
Active sites can close around substrate.

questions.q: Km (Michaelis constant) is:
opts: The substrate concentration at which the enzyme reaches half its maximum velocity
The maximum velocity achieved by the enzyme
questions.exp: Km = [S] at which enzyme velocity is ½ Vmax. Low Km = high affinity for substrate.
optExp: Km is a substrate parameter, not enzyme concentration.

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor affects enzyme kinetics by:
opts: It increases Km while Vmax remains unchanged
It decreases both Km and Vmax
It increases both Km and Vmax
questions.exp: Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site — more substrate restores Vmax, but more is needed to reach ½ Vmax (Km increases).
optExp: Km should INCREASE with competitive inhibition.

questions.q: A non-competitive inhibitor affects enzyme kinetics by:
opts: Binds to the allosteric site, not the active site
Binds to both free enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex
questions.exp: Non-competitive inhibitors bind allosteric sites and cannot be overcome by more substrate. Vmax decreases; Km unchanged.

questions.q: Uncompetitive inhibitors:
opts: Binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex
Decreases both Km and Vmax proportionally
Increases Vmax at higher substrate concentrations
Cannot be overcome by increasing substrate concentration
questions.exp: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, locking the substrate in. Both Km and Vmax decrease.
optExp: Km and Vmax do decrease, but binding only the ES complex is the defining feature.
True but not the defining feature.

questions.q: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the y-intercept equals:
questions.exp: On the double-reciprocal plot, the y-intercept = 1/Vmax and the x-intercept = −1/Km.
optExp: Vmax is not the y-intercept directly.
Km appears as the x-intercept reciprocal.

questions.q: Most human enzymes function optimally at:
questions.exp: Human enzymes evolved at core body temperature (~37°C). Above this, denaturation occurs.
optExp: This is feverish; many enzymes start to denature.

questions.q: An enzyme with a LOW Km has:
opts: Very high Vmax at all times
questions.exp: Low Km = high substrate affinity (e.g. hexokinase). The enzyme operates efficiently at low substrate concentrations.
optExp: Low Km enzymes can still be inhibited.
Km does not indicate cofactor requirement.

questions.q: Which is NOT an irreversible step of glycolysis?
opts: The phosphoglucose isomerase reaction is reversible
The pyruvate kinase reaction is irreversible
questions.exp: The three irreversible steps are hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase. Phosphoglucose isomerase (step 2) is reversible, making it the only reversible step listed.
optExp: Hexokinase IS irreversible — it is one of the three irreversible glycolytic steps.
PFK-1 IS irreversible — the rate-limiting step of glycolysis.
Pyruvate kinase IS irreversible — the final step of glycolysis.
Most glycolytic steps are reversible; only hexokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase are irreversible.

questions.q: Vmax is best defined as:
opts: The maximum velocity achieved at enzyme saturation
The substrate concentration at half-maximal velocity
The minimum velocity ever achieved by the enzyme
The ratio of product formed to substrate consumed
questions.exp: Vmax is the maximum rate when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate.
optExp: Vmax is the MAXIMUM, not minimum.
That is Kd, a different parameter.
That describes k_cat or turnover number.

questions.q: Allosteric enzymes typically show:
opts: Constant velocity regardless of substrate concentration
Inverse relationship between substrate and velocity
questions.exp: Allosteric enzymes (often multi-subunit) show sigmoidal kinetics due to cooperative substrate binding.

questions.q: An irreversible inhibitor:
opts: Can be overcome by adding excess substrate
Forms permanent covalent bonds with the enzyme
Binds reversibly to the allosteric site
Always increases Vmax of the enzyme
Reduces Km while leaving Vmax unchanged
questions.exp: Irreversible inhibitors form covalent bonds and permanently disable the enzyme (e.g. aspirin acetylating COX).
optExp: Cannot be overcome — they are covalently bound.

questions.q: Which TCA enzyme is inhibited by high NADH?
opts: Both citrate synthase and isocitrate dehydrogenase
questions.exp: Both citrate synthase and IDH (and α-KG DH) are inhibited by NADH, which signals high cellular energy state.
optExp: Citrate synthase is inhibited, but so are others.
IDH is inhibited, but so is citrate synthase.

questions.q: Gluconeogenesis produces glucose from non-carbohydrate sources mainly in the:
questions.exp: Gluconeogenesis occurs principally in the liver (and to a smaller extent the kidney cortex), maintaining blood glucose during fasting.
optExp: The brain consumes glucose; cannot make it.
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so cannot release glucose.
The spleen has no significant role in gluconeogenesis.

questions.q: Which of the following substrates is NOT a major gluconeogenic precursor?
questions.exp: Acetyl-CoA cannot be net converted to glucose in humans — there is no enzyme to bypass the irreversible PDH step.
optExp: Lactate (Cori cycle) is a major precursor.
Glycerol from triacylglycerols is a precursor.
Alanine (glucose-alanine cycle) is a major precursor.

questions.q: Which enzyme is unique to gluconeogenesis, bypassing pyruvate kinase?
questions.exp: Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to OAA; PEPCK then converts OAA to PEP, bypassing irreversible pyruvate kinase.
optExp: PDH converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, not gluconeogenic.
Hexokinase makes G6P from glucose, the opposite direction.

questions.q: Which enzyme bypasses PFK-1 in gluconeogenesis?
questions.exp: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase hydrolyses F1,6BP to F6P, the gluconeogenic bypass of PFK-1.
optExp: G6Pase bypasses hexokinase at the final step.

questions.q: Why can't muscle release free glucose into the blood?
opts: Its glucose is sequestered in the glycolytic pathway
questions.exp: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so G6P generated from glycogen cannot be dephosphorylated to free glucose for export.
optExp: Muscle lacks pyruvate carboxylase too, but the key difference is G6Pase.

questions.q: Which hormone promotes glycogenolysis in the liver during fasting?
questions.exp: Glucagon (and adrenaline) activates glycogen phosphorylase via cAMP/PKA, mobilising glucose from glycogen stores.
optExp: Oxytocin acts on uterus and breast.

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting step of glycogen synthesis?
questions.exp: Glycogen synthase is rate-limiting in glycogenesis, activated by insulin (via dephosphorylation).
optExp: Branching enzyme adds α-1,6 branches but isn't rate-limiting.
Provides activated glucose but isn't rate-limiting.

questions.q: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of glycogenolysis?
questions.exp: Glycogen phosphorylase liberates glucose-1-phosphate from glycogen and is rate-limiting; activated by glucagon/adrenaline.

questions.q: In severe liver disease, a patient is most likely to develop:
questions.exp: The liver maintains blood glucose during fasting via gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Severe liver dysfunction → hypoglycaemia.
optExp: Liver may also affect ketone clearance but hypoglycaemia is the key finding.
Lactic acidosis (not alkalosis) is more typical.

questions.q: How many ATP equivalents does the Cori cycle cost the body per glucose recycled?
questions.exp: Muscle gains 2 ATP from anaerobic glycolysis, but the liver uses 6 ATP to remake glucose — a net cost of 4 ATP.

questions.q: Glycogen branches are formed by an α-1,6 glycosidic bond approximately every:
questions.exp: Branching enzyme introduces α-1,6 branches roughly every 8-10 glucose units, increasing solubility and accessibility.

questions.q: The activated form of glucose used to add residues to glycogen is:
questions.exp: UDP-glucose, made by UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase, donates glucose units to growing glycogen chains.
optExp: G6P is the entry point, not the donor.
G1P is the immediate precursor of UDP-glucose.

questions.q: During prolonged fasting, the brain begins to use which alternative fuel?
questions.exp: After a few days of fasting, the brain shifts to using ketone bodies (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate) for ~60% of its energy.
optExp: Fatty acids cannot cross the BBB efficiently.
Amino acids are not the main brain fuel.
Glycerol is too minor a fuel source.

questions.q: Glycogen storage in the liver primarily serves to:
questions.exp: Liver glycogen is broken down to release free glucose into the blood, maintaining blood glucose levels between meals.
optExp: Liver glycogen serves systemic glucose homeostasis, not local ATP.
Glycogen is hydrated but storage isn't for water.
Cholesterol synthesis uses acetyl-CoA, not glycogen directly.

questions.q: Adrenaline activates glycogenolysis in muscle via:
questions.exp: Adrenaline binds β2 receptors on muscle (Gs-coupled), raising cAMP, activating PKA, which activates phosphorylase kinase → glycogen phosphorylase.
optExp: α1 receptors are more on vascular smooth muscle.
Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels.

questions.q: Where does beta-oxidation of fatty acids occur?
questions.exp: Beta-oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix (peroxisomes handle very-long-chain fatty acids).
optExp: Fatty acid synthesis is cytoplasmic, but breakdown is mitochondrial.
Lysosomes degrade macromolecules but not via beta-oxidation.

questions.q: Long-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria via:
questions.exp: Long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs are conjugated to carnitine by CPT-I, transported by translocase, and reformed by CPT-II in the matrix.
optExp: Long chains cannot freely cross the inner membrane.
Sodium-glucose co-transport is for intestinal/renal glucose.

questions.q: Each cycle of beta-oxidation produces:
questions.exp: Each round shortens the fatty acid by 2 carbons, releasing one acetyl-CoA and reducing one FAD and one NAD⁺.
optExp: ATP is not directly produced per cycle.

questions.q: Beta-oxidation is most active in which condition?
opts: Fed state with high insulin levels
questions.exp: Beta-oxidation is upregulated when glucose is low: fasting, prolonged exercise, or starvation.

questions.q: Ketone bodies are produced in the liver from:
questions.exp: Ketogenesis condenses two acetyl-CoA into acetoacetate (and β-hydroxybutyrate), produced when acetyl-CoA exceeds TCA capacity.
optExp: Glucose breakdown does not directly form ketones.
Lactate is recycled via Cori cycle.
Ketogenic amino acids contribute via acetyl-CoA.

questions.q: Which is NOT a ketone body?
opts: All of the above are ketone bodies
questions.exp: The three ketone bodies are acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone. Pyruvate is not a ketone body.
optExp: β-OH-butyrate is the most abundant in DKA.
Acetone gives the breath smell in DKA.
Pyruvate is NOT a ketone body.

questions.q: During lipolysis in adipose tissue, triacylglycerols are broken into:
questions.exp: Hormone-sensitive lipase hydrolyses TAGs into glycerol and free fatty acids, which are released into blood.
optExp: No pyruvate or glucose produced here.
Cholesterol is unrelated to TAG breakdown.

questions.q: In adipose tissue, glycerol released from TAG breakdown is used in the liver for:
questions.exp: Glycerol enters gluconeogenesis via glycerol kinase → glycerol-3-P → DHAP, contributing to blood glucose during fasting.
optExp: Glycerol is not a fatty acid.
Glycogen synthesis happens after glucose is made.

questions.q: Each fatty acid carbon yields more energy than each glucose carbon because:
opts: Fatty acids contain more carbons per molecule
Fatty acids are more reduced than carbohydrates
Fatty acids bypass the electron transport chain
Fatty acids contain more oxygen atoms
questions.exp: Fatty acid carbons are highly reduced, so beta-oxidation generates many more NADH/FADH₂ per carbon.
optExp: Length alone is not the reason — it's per gram efficiency.
Fatty acids feed INTO the ETC, not skip it.
They are largely OXYGEN-poor compared to carbohydrate.

questions.q: In uncontrolled type 1 diabetes leading to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), the metabolic state most resembles:
opts: A fed metabolic state with high insulin levels
questions.exp: DKA mimics fasting/starvation: cells cannot use glucose (no insulin), so beta-oxidation and ketogenesis run unchecked.
optExp: Insulin is absent in DKA, not high.
Anaerobic exercise produces lactate, not ketones primarily.

questions.q: How many amino acids are commonly found in human proteins?
questions.exp: There are 20 standard amino acids encoded by the genetic code, with 9 considered essential in humans.
optExp: 4 is the number of nucleotides in DNA.
Approximate number of essential amino acids.
The alphabet has 26 letters, not amino acids.
64 is the number of codons (including stop).

questions.q: The isoelectric point (pI) of an amino acid is the pH at which it:
opts: It becomes most soluble in water
questions.exp: At the pI, the amino acid exists as a zwitterion with no net charge — solubility is minimal and it does not migrate in an electric field.
optExp: Below pI it carries positive charge.
Above pI it carries negative charge.
Solubility is actually minimal at pI.
While solubility is minimal, this is a consequence, not the definition.

questions.q: Which amino acid is achiral?
questions.exp: Glycine has two hydrogens on its α-carbon, making it the only achiral amino acid.
optExp: Has a methyl side chain — chiral.

questions.q: Which amino acid contains a thiol (-SH) group capable of forming disulfide bonds?
questions.exp: Cysteine has a sulfhydryl (-SH) side chain that forms covalent disulfide bridges with other cysteines, stabilising protein structure.
optExp: Methionine has a thioether (S-CH₃), not a free -SH.
Tyrosine has an aromatic ring with hydroxyl.

questions.q: Normal arterial blood pH is approximately:
questions.exp: Arterial pH is tightly maintained at 7.35-7.45, averaging 7.40.
optExp: Neutral pH — outside biological range for blood.

questions.q: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for the bicarbonate buffer is:
questions.exp: pH = pKa + log([conjugate base]/[weak acid]) = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × pCO₂)) for blood.

questions.q: Which amino acid is positively charged at physiological pH?
questions.exp: Lysine, arginine, and histidine have basic side chains with positive charges at pH 7.4 (histidine partially).

questions.q: A buffer system functions best when:
opts: When pH is far from pKa
questions.exp: Buffering capacity is maximal when pH = pKa, where [HA] = [A⁻] and the system resists pH changes most effectively.
optExp: Buffer is ineffective far from pKa.
Only useful if pKa is near 7.
pKa near 0 means very strong acid — poor buffer.

questions.q: Essential amino acids are those that:
opts: Required only during growth and development phases
Cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained from diet
questions.exp: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised in adequate amounts and must be obtained from the diet. There are 9 essential amino acids in adults.
optExp: They are required throughout life, not just growth.
They ARE used in protein synthesis.
Amino acids are not stored in adipose.

questions.q: A patient with severe vomiting develops which acid-base disturbance?
questions.exp: Loss of gastric HCl causes metabolic alkalosis (loss of H⁺).
optExp: Acidosis is typical of diarrhoea, not vomiting.
There is a clear acid-base shift.

questions.q: Which base pairs with adenine in DNA?
questions.exp: A pairs with T via 2 hydrogen bonds in DNA. In RNA, A pairs with U.
optExp: U is in RNA, not DNA.
Bases don't self-pair in normal DNA.

questions.q: How many hydrogen bonds form between G and C?
questions.exp: G-C pairs form 3 H-bonds, making GC-rich regions more thermodynamically stable than AT-rich.
optExp: A-T has 2 H-bonds via 1 less; 1 is too few.
4 H-bonds not possible between these bases.

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semiconservative because:
opts: Each daughter DNA molecule has two new strands
Each daughter DNA molecule has one old and one new strand
DNA is conserved without any copying occurring
Only half of the DNA molecule is copied during replication
DNA replication occurs randomly rather than in a coordinated manner
questions.exp: Each new double helix contains one original strand serving as a template and one newly synthesised strand.

questions.q: DNA polymerase synthesises new DNA in which direction?
questions.exp: DNA polymerase adds new nucleotides to the 3' OH of the growing strand, so synthesis proceeds 5' → 3'.
optExp: Both strands are synthesised 5' → 3', just differently.

questions.q: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix at the replication fork?
questions.exp: Helicase breaks H-bonds between bases, unwinding the parental DNA at the fork.
optExp: DNA pol synthesises new strand, doesn't unwind.
Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling AHEAD of helicase.

questions.q: Okazaki fragments are joined by:
questions.exp: DNA ligase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds.
optExp: DNA pol I removes RNA primers in prokaryotes.

questions.q: Telomerase is most active in which cell type?
questions.exp: Telomerase adds repetitive TTAGGG sequences to chromosome ends, active in proliferative cells: stem cells, germline, and most cancers.

questions.q: In transcription, RNA polymerase reads the DNA template in which direction?
questions.exp: RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3' → 5' and synthesises RNA 5' → 3'.
optExp: This is the direction of RNA synthesis, not template reading.
The template is the antisense strand.

questions.q: In eukaryotes, post-transcriptional modifications of mRNA include all EXCEPT:
opts: Reverse transcription of mRNA to DNA
questions.exp: Reverse transcription (RNA → DNA) is performed by retroviruses, NOT by eukaryotic cells during normal mRNA maturation.

questions.q: Which of the following is found in RNA but not DNA?
questions.exp: RNA contains uracil instead of thymine. The sugar in RNA is ribose, not deoxyribose.

questions.q: Primary protein structure refers to:
questions.exp: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.

questions.q: Secondary structure is stabilised mainly by:
opts: Ionic bonds between charged side chains
Peptide bonds linking consecutive amino acids
questions.exp: α-helices and β-sheets are stabilised by H-bonds between backbone N-H and C=O groups.

questions.q: Quaternary structure refers to:
opts: Overall three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide
Disulfide bond network throughout the protein
questions.exp: Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits, e.g. haemoglobin (α2β2).
optExp: Disulfide bonds can stabilise but aren't quaternary by definition.

questions.q: Which interaction is NOT typically involved in tertiary structure?
opts: Hydrophobic interactions between nonpolar side chains
Ionic interactions between charged side chains
questions.exp: Peptide bonds link primary structure residues. Tertiary structure relies on side-chain interactions (H-bonds, ionic, hydrophobic, disulfide).

questions.q: Collagen's triple helix is unusual because it contains a high proportion of:
questions.exp: Collagen has a repeating Gly-X-Y motif (often Pro-Hyp), allowing tight triple helix packing.
optExp: Lysine is involved in cross-linking but not the main composition.

questions.q: Denaturation of a protein involves:
opts: Loss of primary amino acid sequence
questions.exp: Denaturation disrupts secondary/tertiary/quaternary structure (e.g. by heat, pH, urea) but leaves peptide bonds intact.
optExp: Hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds, not denaturation.

questions.q: Haemoglobin demonstrates cooperative binding, shown as a:
questions.exp: Haemoglobin's sigmoidal O₂ binding curve reflects positive cooperativity between its 4 subunits.

questions.q: Chaperones (e.g. HSP70) function to:
opts: Catalysing peptide bond formation during translation
Assisting correct protein folding and preventing aggregation
Cleaving signal sequences from nascent proteins
Binding to mRNA molecules during translation
questions.exp: Chaperones prevent misfolding/aggregation and assist proper folding of nascent polypeptides.

questions.q: The α-helix is stabilised by H-bonds between:
opts: Side chains of adjacent amino acid residues
Backbone atoms and surrounding water molecules
Peptide bonds connecting adjacent amino acids
questions.exp: In an α-helix, each backbone C=O H-bonds with the N-H of the residue 4 amino acids ahead.
optExp: Side chains can have interactions but aren't the main α-helix bond.
Water is excluded from inside an α-helix.
Peptide bonds are covalent, not H-bonds.

questions.q: In a globular protein, hydrophobic residues are typically found:
opts: On the protein surface in contact with water
In the hydrophobic core of the protein
Only found in signal peptide sequences
Primarily involved in forming disulfide bonds
questions.exp: Hydrophobic residues cluster in the protein interior, away from water, driving folding via the hydrophobic effect.
optExp: Active sites can be either; not 'hydrophobic only'.

questions.q: In eukaryotes, gene transcription is initiated when RNA polymerase II binds to:
opts: Promoter region upstream of the gene
Terminator sequence at the gene end
questions.exp: RNA Pol II binds the promoter (with help of general transcription factors) to initiate mRNA synthesis.

questions.q: The TATA box is found in the:
opts: In the promoter region upstream of the gene
Near the poly-A tail of mRNA
questions.exp: The TATA box is a core promoter element ~25-30 bp upstream of the start site, bound by TBP.
optExp: TATA box is in promoter, not introns.
Poly-A is at the end of mRNA.

questions.q: Enhancer sequences regulate transcription by:
opts: Binding to ribosomes to regulate translation
Binding transcription factors and looping DNA to increase transcription
questions.exp: Enhancers bind transcription factor activators; the DNA loops to bring them near the promoter, increasing transcription.
optExp: mRNA cleavage is a different process.
Poly-A is added in nucleus by polyA polymerase.

questions.q: Histone acetylation generally:
opts: Tightens chromatin structure, leading to gene silencing
Loosens chromatin structure, leading to gene activation
Has no significant effect on gene expression
questions.exp: Acetylation of histone lysines neutralises positive charges, loosening DNA-histone interaction → euchromatin → transcriptionally active.
optExp: Replication is regulated by different complexes.

questions.q: DNA methylation (typically on CpG islands) usually:
opts: Increases transcription of the affected gene
Causes point mutations in the DNA sequence
Marks the centromere for chromosome segregation
questions.exp: Methylation of cytosines in CpG islands recruits repressors and condenses chromatin, silencing genes.
optExp: Methylation regulates rather than directly mutates.
DNA methylation affects transcription, not translation.

questions.q: In which step of gene expression do introns get removed?
opts: During RNA splicing in the nucleus
questions.exp: Spliceosomes remove introns from pre-mRNA in the nucleus before mature mRNA is exported.
optExp: Introns are removed before mRNA leaves the nucleus.
DNA is not edited like this.

questions.q: How many nucleotides make up a codon?
questions.exp: A codon is a triplet of nucleotides specifying one amino acid (4³ = 64 possible codons).
optExp: A single nucleotide cannot specify 20 amino acids.
4 nucleotides would yield 256 codons — more than needed.

questions.q: The start codon in eukaryotes is:
questions.exp: AUG codes for methionine and is the initiation codon for translation in eukaryotes.
optExp: GUG is a start codon in prokaryotes, but AUG is standard eukaryotic start.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a stop codon?
opts: All of UAA, UAG, and UGA are stop codons
questions.exp: AUG is the START codon. Stop codons are UAA, UAG, UGA.
optExp: This is correct as a statement.

questions.q: tRNAs carry their amino acid attached to:
opts: The 5' end of the tRNA molecule
The 3' CCA end of the tRNA
The D arm of the tRNA
The T arm of the tRNA
questions.exp: Amino acids are esterified to the 3' CCA terminus of tRNA via aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
optExp: Anticodon binds mRNA, doesn't carry amino acid.

questions.q: During translation elongation, the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA binds which ribosomal site?
questions.exp: Incoming aminoacyl-tRNAs enter the A (aminoacyl) site; the growing peptide moves from P to A.
optExp: The P site holds the growing peptide chain.
T site is not a ribosomal site.

questions.q: Peptide bond formation in the ribosome is catalysed by:
opts: Peptidyl transferase activity in ribosomal rRNA
questions.exp: Peptidyl transferase activity is a ribozyme (catalytic RNA) in the large ribosomal subunit.
optExp: This charges tRNA with amino acid.

questions.q: The genetic code is described as 'degenerate' because:
opts: Each codon specifies multiple amino acids
Multiple codons encode the same amino acid
Some codons are skipped during translation
The genetic code differs between prokaryotes and eukaryotes
Codons overlap with each other on mRNA
questions.exp: Most amino acids are encoded by more than one codon, due to wobble base-pairing at the third position.
optExp: Codons are read sequentially without skipping.

questions.q: Polypeptide synthesis proceeds from:
questions.exp: Translation grows the polypeptide from N-terminus to C-terminus while mRNA is read 5' to 3'.

questions.q: Post-translational modifications include all EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Reverse transcription generates DNA from RNA — it is not a post-translational protein modification.

questions.q: Which enzyme is most specific for myocardial infarction in the first 6 hours?
questions.exp: Cardiac troponin I (and T) is the gold-standard cardiac-specific marker, rising 3-6 hours post-MI and lasting up to 10-14 days.

questions.q: In acute pancreatitis, which enzyme is most elevated?
questions.exp: Serum amylase and lipase rise rapidly in acute pancreatitis. Lipase is more specific and persists longer.
optExp: CK is for muscle/heart, less specific.

questions.q: In hepatocellular injury, which liver enzyme is most specific?
questions.exp: ALT is found predominantly in hepatocytes — the most specific marker for hepatocellular injury.
optExp: GGT confirms hepatic origin of ALP but not most specific itself.

questions.q: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over approximately:
opts: One day of average blood glucose
One week of average blood glucose
Two to three months of average blood glucose
Six months of average blood glucose
One year of average blood glucose
questions.exp: HbA1c reflects glycation of haemoglobin over ~2-3 months (the lifespan of red cells).

questions.q: A raised anion gap metabolic acidosis can be caused by all EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Diarrhoea causes a NORMAL anion gap metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate loss). The others add unmeasured anions.

questions.q: In phenylketonuria (PKU), the deficient enzyme is:
questions.exp: PKU is an autosomal recessive disorder of phenylalanine hydroxylase, leading to phenylalanine accumulation and intellectual disability if untreated.
optExp: BCKD deficiency causes maple syrup urine disease.

questions.q: In G6PD deficiency, oxidative haemolysis occurs because:
opts: Cannot regenerate reduced glutathione via NADPH
questions.exp: G6PD generates NADPH via the pentose phosphate pathway, needed to regenerate reduced glutathione and protect RBCs from oxidative damage.

questions.q: Jaundice with predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia suggests:
opts: Gilbert syndrome with mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
questions.exp: Conjugated bilirubin elevation suggests cholestasis/post-hepatic obstruction (stones, tumour, stricture).

questions.q: In hypoglycaemia, which counter-regulatory hormone is released first?
questions.exp: Glucagon is the first-line counter-regulator, rapidly mobilising hepatic glucose via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Adrenaline also rises quickly.
optExp: Cortisol acts later in chronic hypoglycaemia.
Thyroxine is not a rapid responder.

questions.q: Which of the following best indicates renal function?
opts: Creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
questions.exp: Creatinine and eGFR are the standard markers of renal function. Urea is also used but is more variable.

questions.q: In skeletal muscle during exercise, lactate is produced because:
opts: Mitochondria are absent in muscle cells
questions.exp: During intense exercise, glycolysis outpaces oxidative phosphorylation; LDH regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH by reducing pyruvate to lactate.
optExp: Acetyl-CoA inhibition is part of regulation but not the cause.
ATP is being USED, not absent.
TCA continues but capacity is exceeded.

questions.q: Allosteric activators of enzymes typically:
opts: Bind to a regulatory site distant from the active site
Have no effect on enzyme Vmax
questions.exp: Allosteric activators bind regulatory sites distinct from the active site, often shifting the enzyme toward its high-affinity (R) state.
optExp: Substrates and competitive ligands bind active site.

questions.q: A coenzyme differs from a cofactor in that coenzymes are:
opts: Organic molecules that serve as cofactors
questions.exp: Cofactors include both inorganic (metal ions) and organic (coenzymes — often vitamin-derived) helpers. Coenzymes are organic.
optExp: Coenzymes assist but aren't substrates per se.

questions.q: NAD⁺ functions as a:
questions.exp: NAD⁺ accepts electrons (becoming NADH) in catabolic reactions; NADP⁺/NADPH is for biosynthesis.

questions.q: The turnover number (kcat) refers to:
opts: Maximum substrate concentration at enzyme saturation
Number of substrate molecules converted per enzyme molecule per unit time
Maximum reaction velocity of the enzyme
questions.exp: kcat = Vmax/[Etotal] = molecules of substrate converted per enzyme molecule per second at saturation.
optExp: Vmax is rate, not turnover per enzyme.

questions.q: The backbone of DNA is composed of:
questions.exp: DNA backbone = alternating deoxyribose sugars and phosphate groups linked by phosphodiester bonds.
optExp: Histones package DNA but aren't the backbone.

questions.q: A purine includes:
questions.exp: Purines = adenine and guanine (two rings). Pyrimidines = cytosine, thymine, uracil (one ring).

questions.q: A pyrimidine includes:
questions.exp: Pyrimidines have a single ring structure: cytosine (C), thymine (T) and uracil (U). Purines (adenine, guanine) have a double ring.
optExp: Adenine is a purine — double ring structure.
Guanine is a purine — double ring structure.
Ribose is a sugar, not a nitrogenous base.
Adenosine is a nucleoside (adenine + ribose), not a base.

questions.q: The peptide bond is a:
opts: A covalent amide bond between amino acids
An ionic bond between charged atoms
A hydrophobic interaction between side chains
questions.exp: A peptide bond is a covalent amide linkage formed by dehydration synthesis between two amino acids.
optExp: Phosphate esters are in DNA/RNA backbones.

questions.q: Transcription factors regulate gene expression by:
opts: Bind to DNA sequences and recruit RNA polymerase
Cleave DNA strands at specific sites
Form the structural components of ribosomes
questions.exp: Transcription factors bind promoters/enhancers/silencers, recruiting (or blocking) RNA pol II and modifying transcription rates.

questions.q: Polysomes (polyribosomes) are:
opts: Multiple ribosomes translating a single mRNA simultaneously
Multiple DNA strands bound together covalently
Free amino acid chains awaiting incorporation into protein
questions.exp: Multiple ribosomes can translate a single mRNA at the same time, increasing protein output per transcript.
optExp: Mitochondria have their own ribosomes but polysome is the general term.

questions.q: Random blood glucose ≥ 11.1 mmol/L with symptoms is diagnostic of:
questions.exp: WHO/NICE criteria: random ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms, or fasting ≥7.0 mmol/L, or HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%).

questions.q: Cholesterol synthesis occurs primarily in the:
questions.exp: Cholesterol is synthesised in hepatocyte cytoplasm and smooth ER, starting from acetyl-CoA via HMG-CoA reductase (the statin target).
optExp: Peroxisomes handle VLCFAs and bile acid synthesis steps.

questions.q: HMG-CoA reductase is the target of:
questions.exp: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, lowering LDL cholesterol.
optExp: Metformin acts on AMPK / mitochondrial pathways.
Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase.

questions.q: A child with hepatomegaly and severe fasting hypoglycaemia has glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency. This is:
questions.exp: Von Gierke disease (GSD I) = glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, presenting with severe fasting hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia.

questions.q: A patient with a 4-day fast has ketones in the urine because:
questions.exp: Fasting → low insulin, high glucagon → lipolysis → beta-oxidation → excess acetyl-CoA → ketogenesis in the liver.
optExp: OAA is depleted (used for gluconeogenesis), so TCA is limited.
Lactic acidosis is anaerobic glycolysis, not fasting.

questions.q: Lactic acidosis in shock results from:
opts: Insufficient oxygen availability leading to anaerobic metabolism
questions.exp: Tissue hypoxia in shock forces anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactate. Lactic acidosis is a key feature of shock.
optExp: Liver clears lactate; dysfunction worsens but is not the cause.

questions.q: Insulin signalling activates which transporter for glucose uptake into muscle and fat?
questions.exp: GLUT4 is insulin-responsive; insulin → translocation of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane in muscle and adipose tissue.
